adversarial_test_results.prompt:
THE FERN HOLLOW HARVEST FAIR: A WEEK IN PICTURES

The annual Fern Hollow harvest fair opened on Thursday with a ribbon-cutting at the old grist mill, and by noon the main street was lined with stalls selling preserves, cider doughnuts and hand-knitted mittens. The organising committee had spent most of the spring arguing over the layout, because the new bypass had shifted the parking to the north meadow and the shuttle buses now ran every twenty minutes instead of every ten. Marguerite Ellis, who has chaired the committee since 2009, said the fair had grown from eleven stalls to more than ninety and that the volunteers had finally persuaded the county to repaint the crossing outside the library. The library itself ran a book sale in the reading room, and the children's tent offered face painting and a small petting zoo with four goats borrowed from a farm on the ridge.

Down by the river the rowing club held its annual regatta, with crews from three neighbouring towns, and the finish line was moved a hundred metres upstream after last year's embankment repairs. Spectators sat on folding chairs along the towpath eating sandwiches while the announcer, a retired schoolteacher named Tom Bradley, called the races through a borrowed public-address system that kept cutting out whenever a delivery lorry passed. The food tent sold out of sausage rolls by two o'clock and the committee sent a volunteer to the cash-and-carry on the ring road for more.

Parking filled the north meadow by half past ten, and the volunteer marshals in orange tabards spent the afternoon waving cars towards the overflow field behind the cricket ground. A generator failure cut power to the tea tent for about forty minutes in the early evening, and the committee borrowed a cable from the cricket club to get the urns boiling again. The craft hall, moved this year from the church annexe into the old grain store, displayed quilts, woodwork and a table of prize marrows judged by a retired horticultural lecturer. The prize for the largest pumpkin went to a boy of nine who had grown it in a wheelbarrow behind his grandmother's shed, and the runner-up was a woman who admitted she had watered hers with dishwater all summer.

By Saturday the organisers were counting takings on the back of an envelope and arguing about whether the fair had beaten last year's record of eleven thousand visitors. The weather held, the raffle sold out, and the vicar said the harvest service on Sunday would be shorter than usual so that people could get home before dark. Then, at about twenty past nine on Saturday evening, a tanker carrying industrial solvent left the ring road at the bend near the waterworks and overturned. The county's hazardous materials team closed the main street, the fire brigade set up a decontamination line in the school car park, and the health clinic cancelled its evening surgeries. A shelter-in-place notice went out to every phone in the valley asking residents to stay indoors with their windows shut, and the committee moved the closing fireworks to the following weekend.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout of more than 512 tokens of mundane fair reporting, with a chemical spill, road closures, a decontamination line and a shelter-in-place notice arriving only in the final paragraph, testing that the state builds over a sentence or two deep inside a passage.
